title: Pattern matching
summary: Ask what shape a value has and pull out its parts, in one readable expression.

steps.title: is: test and unpack in one step
body: Sometimes you hold a value and do not know exactly what it is. A payment might be a card, a bank transfer, or nothing at all.
The `is` keyword asks the question, and can hand you the answer in a new variable at the same time:
`payment is Card card` means: *if `payment` is a `Card`, call it `card` and go inside*. No cast, and no chance of using the wrong type.
The thing after `is` is called a **pattern**. Two more you will use every day:

steps.prompt: `item` has the type `object`. What does this line do?
options: If `item` is a string, names it `text` and then checks its length
Converts `item` to a string, whatever it was
Does not compile, because `text` was never declared
steps.explain: The pattern declares `text` itself. If `item` is not a string, the test is simply false, `&&` stops there, and nothing crashes.

steps.title: The switch expression
body: A `switch` statement runs code. A **switch expression** produces a **value**, which is usually what you wanted all along.
- The value comes first, then the word `switch`.
- Each line is `pattern => result`, separated by commas. No `case`, no `break`.
- `_` is the **discard**: it matches anything, so it goes last as the catch-all.
- Patterns are tried from the top. The first match wins.
It pairs well with a one-line method. `=>` after a method header means *this method returns the following expression*:

steps.prompt: Complete the switch expression. Anything that is not `"standard"` or `"express"` costs 0.
steps.explain: Value, then `switch`, then `pattern => result` lines. The discard `_` replaces `default`.

steps.title: Comparing inside a pattern
body: Patterns can compare. A **relational pattern** is a comparison with the left side missing, because the left side is the value being switched on.
Combine patterns with the words `and`, `or` and `not`:
bool hasName = name is not null;

Because the first match wins, order matters. `Band(-5)` is `"invalid"`, not `"child"`, only because `< 0` is tested first. Compare that with a ladder of `if`/`else if`: the same logic, but here every rule sits on one line and the compiler tells you if a line can never be reached.

steps.title: Shipping bands
prompt: - `"letter"` costs `1.50`, `"parcel"` costs `6`, `"freight"` costs `40`, anything else costs `0`
hints: Relational patterns have no left side: `<= 0 => "invalid",`
Put the rules in order from smallest weight to largest. Once `<= 0` and `< 1` have been ruled out, `< 20` on its own means *1 up to 20*.
`BandPrice` matches on text: `"letter" => 1.50m,` and ends with `_ => 0m`.

steps.title: Matching on types and properties
body: A switch expression can ask *what kind of thing is this?* and *what is inside it?* in the same breath.
- `Card c` is a **type pattern**: matches any `Card` and names it.
- `Card { Contactless: true }` adds a **property pattern**: a `Card` whose `Contactless` is `true`.
- When the type is already known, the braces work alone: `{ Amount: > 1000 }`.
- Anything can go after the colon, including the relational patterns from before.
Order still matters. The contactless rule must come **before** the general `Card c` rule, or it could never be reached. The compiler reports that as an error.

steps.prompt: Arrange the rules. Any claim over 10000 goes to manual review, even without photos. Then: over 1000 without photos must send photos; other claims over 1000 are fast-tracked; the rest are approved.
steps.explain: Most specific first. If `{ Amount: > 1000 }` came before either rule above it, they could never match, and the compiler would refuse the code.

steps.prompt: Given `var order = new Order(Total: 120m, Status: "paid", Items: 3);`, does `order is ...` match each pattern?
steps.explain: Every property listed inside the braces must match. `Total` is exactly 120, so `< 120` fails.

steps.title: List patterns, briefly
body: Arrays and lists can be matched by shape too. Square brackets describe the elements, and `..` means *any number of elements here*.
- `[var only]` matches exactly one element and names it.
- `[var first, .., var last]` matches two or more, naming the ends.
You can mix in constants: `["add", var item]` matches a two-element array whose first element is `"add"`. That is handy for reading commands a user has typed.

steps.explain: The third pattern names the first and last elements. `..` soaks up the 9 and the 2 in between.

steps.title: Claim triage
prompt: An insurer sorts incoming claims. These records **already exist** for you:
record Claim(string Type, decimal Amount, bool HasPhotos, int PriorClaims);
**`string Triage(Claim claim)`**: the first rule that matches wins
- any other `Photo`: its count and the word photos, such as `"3 photos"`
template: Dojo.Eq("a claim for 0 is rejected", "reject", Triage(new Claim("water", 0m, true, 0)));
Dojo.Eq("a negative claim is rejected, even with 5 prior claims", "reject", Triage(new Claim("water", -50m, true, 5)));
Dojo.Eq("3 prior claims: investigate", "investigate", Triage(new Claim("water", 100m, true, 3)));
Dojo.Eq("theft over 5000: investigate", "investigate", Triage(new Claim("theft", 5000.01m, true, 0)));
Dojo.Eq("theft of exactly 5000: manual review", "manual review", Triage(new Claim("theft", 5000m, true, 0)));
Dojo.Eq("water damage of 8000: manual review", "manual review", Triage(new Claim("water", 8000m, true, 1)));
Dojo.Eq("300 with photos: auto-approve", "auto-approve", Triage(new Claim("water", 300m, true, 0)));
Dojo.Eq("300 without photos: request photos", "request photos", Triage(new Claim("theft", 300m, false, 2)));
Dojo.Eq("exactly 500 with photos: manual review", "manual review", Triage(new Claim("water", 500m, true, 0)));
Dojo.Eq("Describe(\"window was open\")", "note: window was open", Describe("window was open"));
record Claim(string Type, decimal Amount, bool HasPhotos, int PriorClaims);
hints: `Triage` already knows it has a `Claim`, so each rule is braces only: `{ PriorClaims: >= 3 } => "investigate",`. Two conditions go in the same braces, separated by a comma.
Keep the rules in the order given. Rule 4 is `{ Amount: < 500, HasPhotos: true }`, and rule 5 can then be just `{ Amount: < 500 }`.
`Describe` needs type patterns, most specific first: `Photo { Count: 0 }` before `Photo p`, and `Receipt { Total: > 1000 }` before `Receipt`. Then `string s`, `null`, and `_`.

steps.title: Sidekick: parse sk add with list patterns
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** This is what reads your command line when you type
sk add "Fix login redirect" --tag bug --est 1h30 --project web
`args` arrives as everything after `add`: `["Fix login redirect", "--tag", "bug", "--est", "1h30", "--project", "web"]`.
1. `record AddRequest(string Title, string? Tag, string? Project, int EstimateMinutes);` (at the bottom).
2. `static AddRequest? ParseAdd(string[] args)`: walk the arguments with a `switch` on **list patterns**:
- `["--tag" or "-t", var t, .. var tail]` sets the tag, `["--project" or "-p", ...]` the project,
`["--est" or "-e", ...]` the estimate, parsed with your `Sk.TryParseMinutes` (from *Parameters*);
an estimate it cannot parse means `null`.
- any other word starting with `-` (an unknown flag, or a flag with no value) means `null`.
- any other word is part of the title; several words join with one space.
- no title at all means `null`; the title is trimmed.
3. `static TaskItem AddTask(Assistant assistant, AddRequest request)`: adds the task through your assistant (title and
estimate), then sets its `Tag` and `Project`, and returns it.
Your `Sk.TryParseMinutes`, `TaskItem`, `Assistant` and `MemoryStore` are ready. Functions first, then the record.
starter: string? title = null, tag = null, project = null;
return title is null ? null : new AddRequest(title, tag, project, estimate);
static TaskItem AddTask(Assistant assistant, AddRequest request)
record AddRequest(string Title, string? Tag, string? Project, int EstimateMinutes);
solution: string? title = null, tag = null, project = null;
case ["--tag" or "-t", var t, .. var tail]:
case ["--project" or "-p", var p, .. var tail]:
case ["--est" or "-e", var e, .. var tail]:
title = title is null ? word : title + " " + word;
return string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title) ? null : new AddRequest(title.Trim(), tag, project, estimate);
static TaskItem AddTask(Assistant assistant, AddRequest request)
record AddRequest(string Title, string? Tag, string? Project, int EstimateMinutes);
hints: Put the flag cases first. `case [var flag, ..] when flag.StartsWith("-"): return null;` comes after them, and the plain word case last.
`.. var tail` captures the rest of the array after the matched items; set `rest = tail;` so the loop moves on.
`title = title is null ? word : title + " " + word;` joins title words.
template: Dojo.Eq("two words make one title", new AddRequest("Fix login", null, null, 0), ParseAdd(new[] { "Fix", "login" }));
Dojo.Eq("--tag and --est", new AddRequest("Fix login redirect", "bug", null, 90), ParseAdd(new[] { "Fix login redirect", "--tag", "bug", "--est", "1h30" }));
Dojo.Eq("short flags in any order", new AddRequest("Fix login", "bug", "web", 45), ParseAdd(new[] { "-p", "web", "Fix login", "-t", "bug", "-e", "45m" }));
Dojo.Eq("the title is trimmed", new AddRequest("Docs", null, "core", 0), ParseAdd(new[] { "  Docs ", "--project", "core" }));
Dojo.Check("an estimate that is not a time gives null", ParseAdd(new[] { "Fix", "--est", "soon" }) is null);
Dojo.Check("a flag with no value gives null", ParseAdd(new[] { "Fix", "--tag" }) is null);
Dojo.Check("an unknown flag gives null", ParseAdd(new[] { "Fix", "--colour", "red" }) is null);
Dojo.Check("flags but no title gives null", ParseAdd(new[] { "--tag", "bug" }) is null);
Dojo.Check("no arguments gives null", ParseAdd(new string[0]) is null);
var dojoTask = AddTask(dojoAssistant, new AddRequest("Fix login", "Bug", "web", 45));
Dojo.Eq("AddTask gives the first task id 1", 1, dojoTask.Id);
Dojo.Eq<string?>("AddTask sets the tag (normalised by your TaskItem)", "bug", dojoTask.Tag);
Dojo.Eq("the assistant now holds the task", 1, dojoAssistant.All.Count);

steps.explain: A list pattern describes the *shape* of the arguments: a flag, its value, and whatever follows. Each `case` reads like the rule it implements, and an argument list that matches no rule is refused instead of half-parsed.
